items.stem: Explain the nutrient cycle of the tropical rainforest.
items.answer: Large biomass store; rapid leaf fall all year; small litter store because decomposition is fast in hot, humid conditions; nutrients released quickly and taken up by shallow roots and mycorrhizae; small soil store due to leaching; little loss when undisturbed.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per store/transfer [4]

items.stem: Explain the structure of the tropical rainforest.
items.answer: Layers (emergents, canopy, understorey, shrub layer, forest floor) result from competition for light; tall straight trunks, buttress roots, drip-tip leaves, lianas and epiphytes are adaptations.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per feature explained [4]

items.stem: In a Gersmehl model for a temperate deciduous forest, the nutrient stores hold: biomass 38%, litter 10%, soil 52% of a total of 3 000 kg of nutrients per hectare. Explain the relative size of the litter store.
items.answer: Fairly large: seasonal leaf fall in autumn and slower decomposition in cool winters.

items.stem: In a Gersmehl model for a tropical rainforest, the nutrient stores hold: biomass 77%, litter 3%, soil 20% of a total of 800 kg of nutrients per hectare. (a) Calculate the ratio of the biomass store to the soil store. (b) Explain the relative size of the litter store.
items.answer: (a) 3.85 : 1 (b) Very small: rapid decomposition in constant heat and humidity, so litter is broken down within weeks.

items.stem: “The tropical rainforest is a fragile ecosystem.” Discuss.
items.answer: For: Nutrients held in biomass are lost on clearance; soils leach and erode; species are highly specialised; recovery takes centuries; tipping-point risk in the Amazon. Against: High productivity and rapid regrowth (secondary forest), large genetic diversity and complex food webs give resilience to small disturbances; shifting cultivation was sustainable at low densities. Conclusion: Rainforests are resilient to small-scale disturbance but fragile when cleared on a large scale, because of their nutrient cycle and soils.

items.stem: Explain why rainforest soils become infertile rapidly after clearance.
items.answer: The nutrient store in biomass is removed; heavy rain leaches remaining nutrients and erodes topsoil; laterite may form on exposure; litter supply stops.

items.stem: Explain how savanna vegetation is adapted to the climate.
items.answer: Grasses die back in the dry season and regrow from roots; trees are deciduous, have small leathery leaves, thorns, deep tap roots and thick bark; baobabs store water; acacias have umbrella crowns.

items.stem: Explain the role of fire in the savanna ecosystem.
items.answer: Fire (natural lightning and human burning) removes dead grass and woody seedlings, maintains grassland, releases nutrients as ash, stimulates new growth and germination; fire-resistant species dominate.

items.stem: Ravi argues that human activity is more important than climate in maintaining savanna vegetation. How far do you agree? Support your answer with examples.
items.answer: For: Burning by farmers and pastoralists, grazing and clearance maintain grassland and prevent woodland; fire-climax savannas. items.stem: Explain the formation of savanna soils.
items.answer: Seasonal rainfall leaches nutrients in the wet season; upward capillary movement in the dry season; iron oxides accumulate, sometimes forming hard laterite crusts; limited humus because fire and termites remove litter.

items.stem: Explain the process of secondary succession in a tropical rainforest clearing.
items.answer: Fast-growing pioneers colonise the gap; they shade the ground and add litter; shade-tolerant species grow beneath and eventually overtop them; biodiversity and biomass increase towards a climax over decades to centuries.

Nearby primary forest has about 400 t/ha. Suggest why species richness may take longer to recover than biomass.
items.answer: Many climax species have heavy seeds dispersed by animals that need nearby forest; specialists require mature conditions.

items.stem: Outline the evidence that supports, and the evidence that challenges, the view that the concept of a climatic climax is of limited use in understanding tropical vegetation.
items.answer: For: Fire, grazing, shifting cultivation and logging have modified most tropical vegetation; many savannas are plagioclimaxes; climate itself has changed. Against: The idea explains the broad zonal pattern (rainforest to savanna to desert) and the direction of succession on cleared land. Conclusion: The concept is a useful model of the potential vegetation, but most tropical vegetation is a product of human and natural disturbance.

items.stem: What is meant by the term “succession”?
options: The sequence of changes in plant communities over time on a site.
One of the stages in a plant succession.
A plant community prevented from reaching its climatic climax by human activity such as burning or grazing.
The final, stable plant community in equilibrium with the climate of an area.
items.answer: The sequence of changes in plant communities over time on a site.
items.markingKey: Succession: the sequence of changes in plant communities over time on a site. [1]

items.stem: Explain why recovered secondary forest differs from primary forest.
items.answer: Lower biodiversity and biomass for many decades; fewer emergents; different species mix dominated by pioneers; soils degraded.

items.stem: Kwame argues that the concept of a climatic climax is of limited use in understanding tropical vegetation. How far do you agree? Support your answer with examples.
items.answer: For: Fire, grazing, shifting cultivation and logging have modified most tropical vegetation; many savannas are plagioclimaxes; climate itself has changed. Against: The idea explains the broad zonal pattern (rainforest to savanna to desert) and the direction of succession on cleared land. Conclusion: The concept is a useful model of the potential vegetation, but most tropical vegetation is a product of human and natural disturbance.

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “the transfer of nutrients between the biomass, litter and soil stores of an ecosystem”.
items.answer: Nutrient cycle
items.markingKey: Nutrient cycle: the transfer of nutrients between the biomass, litter and soil stores of an ecosystem. [1]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) In a class discussion, a student says: “Decomposition in the rainforest is very rapid.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) A revision website states: “Tropical rainforests have high biodiversity.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Correct. Constant heat and moisture allow decomposers to break litter down within weeks. (b) Correct. They contain over half of the world’s terrestrial species in about 6% of its land area.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2] (b) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) A student writes: “The lush vegetation of rainforests shows that their soils are very fertile.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) In a class discussion, a student says: “Decomposition in the rainforest is very rapid.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Not correct. Nutrients are held mainly in the biomass; the soils are leached and poor. (b) Correct. Constant heat and moisture allow decomposers to break litter down within weeks.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2] (b) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) In a class discussion, a student says: “Decomposition in the rainforest is very rapid.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) Explain the nutrient cycle of the tropical rainforest.
items.answer: (a) Correct. Constant heat and moisture allow decomposers to break litter down within weeks. (b) Large biomass store; rapid leaf fall all year; small litter store because decomposition is fast in hot, humid conditions; nutrients released quickly and taken up by shallow roots and mycorrhizae; small soil store due to leaching; little loss when undisturbed.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2] (b) 1 mark per store/transfer [4]

items.stem: In a Gersmehl model for a savanna grassland, the nutrient stores hold: biomass 29%, litter 5%, soil 66% of a total of 2 000 kg of nutrients per hectare. Explain the relative size of the litter store.
items.answer: Small in savanna because fire and termites remove litter quickly.

items.stem: In a Gersmehl model for a tropical rainforest, the nutrient stores hold: biomass 76%, litter 5%, soil 19% of a total of 1 200 kg of nutrients per hectare. Calculate the mass of nutrients in each store.
items.answer: biomass 912; litter 60; soil 228 kg/ha

items.stem: In a Gersmehl model for a temperate deciduous forest, the nutrient stores hold: biomass 45%, litter 12%, soil 43% of a total of 1 500 kg of nutrients per hectare. (a) Calculate the mass of nutrients in each store. (b) Calculate the ratio of the biomass store to the soil store.
items.answer: (a) biomass 675; litter 180; soil 645 kg/ha (b) 1.05 : 1

items.stem: In a Gersmehl model for a temperate deciduous forest, the nutrient stores hold: biomass 40%, litter 12%, soil 48% of a total of 800 kg of nutrients per hectare. (a) Calculate the ratio of the biomass store to the soil store. (b) Explain what would happen to the nutrient stores if the vegetation were cleared and burned.
items.answer: (a) 0.83 : 1 (b) Biomass store removed (some nutrients released as ash, briefly enriching soil); with no canopy, heavy rain leaches and erodes the soil; the litter input stops; the cycle collapses.
items.markingKey: (a) 40 ÷ 48 [1] (b) 1 mark per point [3]

items.answer: Deciduous (in the dry season)

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain the role of fire in the savanna ecosystem. (b) Explain the formation of savanna soils.
items.answer: (a) Fire (natural lightning and human burning) removes dead grass and woody seedlings, maintains grassland, releases nutrients as ash, stimulates new growth and germination; fire-resistant species dominate. (b) Seasonal rainfall leaches nutrients in the wet season; upward capillary movement in the dry season; iron oxides accumulate, sometimes forming hard laterite crusts; limited humus because fire and termites remove litter.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark per point [3] (b) [3]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain how savanna vegetation is adapted to the climate. (b) A revision website states: “Savannas have the same NPP as rainforests.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Grasses die back in the dry season and regrow from roots; trees are deciduous, have small leathery leaves, thorns, deep tap roots and thick bark; baobabs store water; acacias have umbrella crowns. (b) Not correct. NPP is about 900 g/m²/yr, much lower than rainforest, because of the dry season.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark per adaptation explained [4] (b) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Researchers recorded mean annual rainfall and woody (tree) cover at 8 savanna sites in East Africa. Table 1.2 gives, for each site, the mean annual rainfall (mm) and the tree cover (%). Site 1: 372, 51. Site 2: 492, 24. Site 3: 524, 33. Site 4: 788, 31. Site 5: 945, 2. Site 6: 953, 13. Site 7: 1127, 57. Site 8: 1199, 60. Critical values of rs for n = 8: 0.643 (0.05 level) and 0.833 (0.01 level). Suggest one limitation of the method and how the investigation could be improved.
items.answer: Fire frequency, grazing and soils also vary between sites; record and control for these, and use more sites from one region.

items.stem: What is meant by the term “climatic climax community”?

The final, stable plant community in equilibrium with the climate of an area.
A plant community prevented from reaching its climatic climax by human activity such as burning or grazing.
Succession on land where vegetation has been removed but soil remains, such as abandoned farmland.

items.answer: (a) Correct. High temperatures and rainfall support rapid growth. (b) Not correct. Climax communities change with climate change and natural disturbances.
